# Why Is It Difficult to Stop?

> "Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin."
>
> — John 8:34

Sooner or later, every man with this habit gets the creepy feeling that he isn't the one in charge of it.

It doesn't begin that way. In the early years the line is casual: "I'll stop. Just not tonight." Augustine, long before he was a saint, prayed much the same prayer: "Give me chastity and continency, only not yet." Sixteen centuries later we're all still praying it.

Then the line changes. After enough failed attempts you decide the fault must be in you. "I just don't have the willpower." Or you decide the fault is in nature: "Men are built this way. There must be something in it that I can't live without."

Trying to quit feels like climbing a sand dune. You dig in and gain a few yards, and you can nearly see over the top. Then comes a bad day, your footing goes, and you slide down to the bottom with sand in your shoes. One man described it exactly:

> "I keep seeing myself it again even after saying it's over."
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

Another wrote:

> "I have struggled with this for all my life I can go a couple of weeks then I right back too it?"
>
> — another commenter on the same blog

Notice the question mark on the end of that. Nobody in the trap can explain it. They only know where they keep ending up.

## Two questions {-}

Find any man who jerks off regularly and ask him: "Suppose you could go back to the week before you first did it, knowing everything you know today. Would you start?"

"NOT A CHANCE."

Now find the man who defends it. He's read that it's natural, he'll tell you that doctors have no problem with it, and he thinks this book is medieval. Ask him: "So you'll be teaching your son to do it every night until he's forty? You'd be pleased to hear it's the one thing that gets him to sleep?"

"OF COURSE NOT."

Isn't that strange? Here is something millions of men do, many of them daily, and not one would choose it again or wish it on his boy.

So the puzzle in this book was never how stopping could be easy. The puzzle is why stopping seems hard, and under that sits a bigger one: why does anybody do it at all?

Think about how you started. Nobody sold it to you. Nobody passed you one behind the bike sheds. Your own body turned up one day with a new trick, and the jokes at school told you that every boy was at it, so you thought no more about it. And then you spent the next ten, twenty or thirty years wishing you could leave it alone, never mentioning it to a soul, and assuming you were the only man in your church who couldn't.

You're not unique. You're standard issue.

Look at what the habit actually gives you in return. What kind of pleasure is it that you regret before you've even got your breath back, and are planning again by the following evening? You wish you weren't doing it while you do it. You're restless for it when you don't. FitXFearless, who did it for years, describes the moment every man knows: "you finish and you just like why did I do that".

And the regret piles up. A man despises himself a little every time he promises God "never again" on Sunday and breaks it on Monday. He despises himself when his wife is asleep in the next room. He despises himself when he's too flat to get out of bed and do the thing he'd planned. A sensible, capable man, who runs every other part of his life well, carries this small contempt for himself everywhere, like a stone in his pocket.

What does he get for carrying it? One man who looked back over half his life gave the honest answer:

> "I wasted 20 years using porn and masturbating. It got me nothing but further away from God."
>
> — a man on a Christian recovery blog

Nothing. That's the going rate.

## The usual explanations {-}

"Fine," you say. "I know all that. But once you're in it, it's very hard to get out."

Why, though? What exactly makes it hard?

**Some say the urges are unbearable.** They aren't. As you'll see next chapter, the urge on its own is a mild, restless itch. You've sat through worse in a dentist's waiting room. Plenty of men have carried this habit to the grave without once suspecting they were hooked on anything, which tells you how gentle the pull really is.

**Some say a man's body needs it.** Pressure builds, they tell you, and it has to go somewhere. But your body was dealing with all of that on its own before you ever lent a hand, and it still knows how. You've also gone days without, on trips and in busy weeks, and nothing burst.

**Some say they simply enjoy it.** I enjoy a good steak. I have never needed a steak every night behind a locked door, and nobody has ever seen me panic at the thought of a week without one. With the things we truly enjoy, we enjoy them while they last and don't sit around feeling robbed in between.

Then come the smaller excuses:

- "It relaxes me." Then why are you wound up again by tomorrow night?
- "It's a release." A release from what? Whatever it was, is it gone?
- "It helps me sleep." How did you sleep when you were nine?
- "It's just a high sex drive." Then why does it happen when you're bored, or sad, or putting off an email, and not aroused at all?
- "It stops me doing something worse." Since when did feeding an appetite shrink it?

Many men say it fills an empty hour. But boredom is a state of mind, and this habit manufactures it. A man who can switch on a thrill in ninety seconds soon finds everything slower than ninety seconds dull. He ends up bored by his own life.

And some fall back on "everybody does it". If everybody treated a headache by hitting himself with a hammer, would you queue up?

## "It's just a habit" {-}

When all the other explanations have collapsed, most men settle on this one: it's only a habit, and habits are hard to break.

It sounds like an answer, but it isn't one. It's what's left on the table once the proper answers have gone.

Are habits hard to break? You change them constantly. You move house, and for two days your hand goes to the wrong wall for the light switch, and by the weekend it doesn't. You rent a car in a country that drives on the opposite side, and after one nervous roundabout you're fine. You start a new job and your whole morning is rearranged within a week. People drop habits of thirty years' standing with no drama whatever, including habits they liked.

So why would this one be different? Here's a habit that leaves you restless when you skip it and ashamed when you don't, a habit you'd pay good money to be rid of, and stopping asks nothing of you. You don't have to do a thing. You only have to not do one. Why can't you?

Because it isn't a habit. Augustine watched it happen in himself and wrote down the stages: "a lust served, became custom; and custom not resisted, became necessity." Custom is the old word for habit. Notice that he doesn't stop there. The thing begins as a wish, hardens into a habit, and ends as something else.

Jesus had the right word for it two thousand years ago, and it's the verse that opens this chapter: a bondservant. A slave. A man with a habit is in charge of it. This thing is in charge of you. You may call that sin, or addiction, or a trap; this book will use all three, and "the habit" as well, for convenience. But never forget what it is. IT'S A MASTER, NOT A HABIT.

That is why it seems so hard to "give up". The slave has come to believe his master is also his comforter: that he gets a real pleasure or a real prop out of it, and that life without it would have a hole in the middle.

Here is the good news. Once you see how the master actually holds you, and why you really reach for it, you'll stop. Just like that. A few weeks from now the only mystery left will be how it ever had a grip on you, and why you can't get your friends to see what you see.

## The sinister trap {-}

This trap is one of the neatest ever built. Your own flesh supplies the bait, and the world stands round telling you it isn't a trap at all.

Think about how a boy walks in. With cigarettes there's at least a cough, and a health warning printed on the box. With porn there's the jolt of knowing he's looking at something he shouldn't. Here there's nothing of the kind. There's no dealer and no price. He doesn't get a hangover or a smell on his clothes, and no other person is involved. It's his own body, in his own bed, and it happened half by accident. No alarm bell rings. Why would one?

By the time something does feel wrong (the first guilt, the first prayer he doesn't quite want to finish), the routine is already laid down. From then on he lives like every other man in the trap. He wonders why he keeps doing it, hopes his own boys never start, and every so often tries to break out.

Now look at when he tries. A man almost never decides to stop on a good day. He decides after an incident: he's nearly caught, or a sermon lands, or he looks at his wife and feels like a fraud, or he's with a real woman and his body lets him down. So he quits on the very day he feels worst, which is the very day his old comforter is the thing he most wants. He has piled a second misery on the first one and thrown away the only remedy he knows.

A few days of that and his resolve goes soft. "I picked a bad week. I'll do it when things calm down. After the exams. When I've got a girlfriend. Once I'm married." Then things do calm down, and with the pressure off, the reason to stop has gone as well. He drifts on until the next incident.

And each year the calm weeks seem fewer. He's left home, there's a job, rent, a wife, small children. Life, he decides, just gets more stressful as you go.

It doesn't. He's mixing up responsibility with stress. You weren't carefree at fourteen; you were a bag of nerves. What has grown is the habit's share of the load. Jerking off doesn't calm a man down. It winds him up, quietly, one guilty night at a time: another secret to keep, another promise broken, another morning started in the red. He blames the job.

Even the men who get out by sheer effort aren't safe. They'll live clean and happy for months or years, and then one low evening walk straight back in. FitXFearless once titled a video "I RELAPSED AFTER 2+ YEARS OF NOFAP { I FEEL HORRIBLE }". That's two years, and he was back to day one.

The whole business is like one of those trick knots. Pull at it with all your strength and it only tightens, and you can strain at it for years. But let someone show you how it's tied, and it falls open in your hands, and you can't believe you ever fought it. This book shows you how it's tied. Your part is to follow each instruction, in order, and not to race through. Skip a step and the knot stays shut.

## The two causes {-}

Stopping can be easy for any man. But first we need the facts, and I don't mean the frightening kind. You've had plenty of those, and if they worked you'd be free already. We need the facts about why you're still doing it. It comes down to two things:

1. **The flesh.**
2. **The world's lies.**

The next two chapters take them in turn.

Men who jerk off are not stupid. In every other department they're sharp, and it's because they're sharp that they put so much effort into their excuses. Underneath the excuses they know the truth. They know they got on perfectly well without it as boys. They never lay awake at nine years old needing it.

The most irritating part is the men who have walked out, and who aren't missing a thing. They aren't gritting their teeth or looking back with longing. If anything they seem faintly puzzled that they ever bothered.

Before long you'll be one of them. Two verses before the one that opens this chapter, Jesus gave the whole method in a single line: "You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free." (John 8:32). If you're an atheist, play along. You don't have to believe who said it to notice that it works.
